final_proof:
Proof. We first prove the result when both measures are finite. Put λ=μ+ν. Then λ is finite. On the real Hilbert space L²(λ), define T(f)=∫_X f dν. This is well-defined and bounded: by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, |T(f)|≤ν(X)^(1/2)(∫_X |f|² dν)^(1/2)≤ν(X)^(1/2)‖f‖_{L²(λ)}. Hence the Hilbert-space Riesz representation theorem gives h∈L²(λ) such that T(f)=∫_X fh dλ for every f∈L²(λ). Since λ is finite, every indicator 1_A belongs to L²(λ), and therefore

ν(A)=∫_A h dλ  (A∈Σ).  (1)

We next determine the range of h. Since the left side of (1) is nonnegative for every A, h≥0 λ-almost everywhere: otherwise one of the sets {h≤−1/n} would have positive λ-measure and would have a strictly negative integral of h. Moreover, because λ(A)−ν(A)=μ(A), equation (1) gives

μ(A)=∫_A (1−h) dλ  (A∈Σ).  (2)

Thus 1−h≥0 λ-almost everywhere by the same argument, so h≤1 λ-almost everywhere. Let N={h=1}. By (2), μ(N)=0. The hypothesis ν≪μ then gives ν(N)=0, and consequently λ(N)=μ(N)+ν(N)=0. After changing h on a λ-null set, we may therefore suppose that 0≤h<1 everywhere. Define

g=h/(1−h).

This is a finite, nonnegative, Σ-measurable function. Equation (2) says that μ has density 1−h with respect to λ. Consequently, for every nonnegative measurable φ,

∫_X φ dμ=∫_X φ(1−h) dλ;

indeed, this follows first for indicators from (2), then for nonnegative simple functions by linearity, and finally for all nonnegative measurable functions by monotone convergence. Taking φ=1_A g and using (1), we obtain

∫_A g dμ=∫_A g(1−h) dλ=∫_A h dλ=ν(A).

This proves existence in the finite-measure case.

We now pass to the σ-finite case. Choose measurable sets P_i and Q_j such that X=⋃_{i≥1}P_i=⋃_{j≥1}Q_j, with μ(P_i)<∞ and ν(Q_j)<∞. Enumerate the countable family {P_i∩Q_j:i,j≥1} as C_1,C_2,…, and make it disjoint by setting E_1=C_1 and E_n=C_n∖⋃_{k<n}C_k for n≥2. Then the E_n are pairwise disjoint measurable sets whose union is X, and both μ(E_n) and ν(E_n) are finite. On the measurable subspace E_n, the restricted measure ν|_{E_n} is absolutely continuous with respect to μ|_{E_n}. The finite case therefore supplies a nonnegative measurable function g_n on E_n such that

ν(A∩E_n)=∫_{A∩E_n} g_n dμ  (A∈Σ).  (3)

Define g on X by g(x)=g_n(x) when x∈E_n. This function is Σ-measurable because the E_n form a countable measurable partition. For A∈Σ, monotone convergence applied to the increasing finite partial sums over this partition, followed by (3) and countable additivity of ν, gives the extended-real equalities

∫_A g dμ=∑_{n=1}^∞ ∫_{A∩E_n} g_n dμ=∑_{n=1}^∞ ν(A∩E_n)=ν(A).

Thus the required density exists.

It remains to prove uniqueness. Suppose g_1 and g_2 are nonnegative measurable functions satisfying ∫_A g_1 dμ=∫_A g_2 dμ=ν(A) for every A∈Σ. By σ-finiteness of ν, choose measurable F_j with X=⋃_{j≥1}F_j and ν(F_j)<∞. For j,m≥1, put

D_{j,m}=F_j∩{g_1≥g_2+1/m}.

Because ν(D_{j,m})≤ν(F_j)<∞, the defining integral identities and the pointwise inequality on D_{j,m} yield

ν(D_{j,m})=∫_{D_{j,m}}g_1 dμ≥∫_{D_{j,m}}g_2 dμ+(1/m)μ(D_{j,m})=ν(D_{j,m})+(1/m)μ(D_{j,m}).

The common ν-value is finite, so μ(D_{j,m})=0. Since the functions take finite values,

{g_1>g_2}=⋃_{j=1}^∞⋃_{m=1}^∞D_{j,m},

and hence μ({g_1>g_2})=0. Interchanging g_1 and g_2 likewise gives μ({g_2>g_1})=0. Therefore g_1=g_2 μ-almost everywhere, as claimed.
